notes: Own.NET#266 slice 2, step 0. The VOCABULARY is frozen; no mapper exists.
The unit of analysis is one occurrence in revision A mapped to revision B.
pattern_id collides on purpose and occurrence_id cannot span runs, so lineage
is precisely the relation neither of those ids carries - and it is EARNED by
Absence of mapping evidence is 'unresolved', on EITHER side. It is not 'new',
not 'ended', and not the same lineage. Same invariant as finding-occurrence/v1
('identity is refused, not approximated') and as the runtime witness ('absence
of a record is not a semantic outcome').
revision_note: This contract was corrected before it was ever merged, under review of PR #65.
The first draft let 'ended' and 'new' be justified by no-mapping-evidence, and
gave 'unresolved' only an A-side anchor - so every unmatched B occurrence was
pushed toward 'new'. That is the fabricated-birth defect the contract exists to
forbid, written into the contract itself. It is fixed in place rather than as a
v2 because v1 has never been implemented or released: nothing is built on it.

continued.means: exactly one successor, established by evidence

branched.forbids: picking a winner and discarding the rest; letting one successor inherit the predecessor's id, which is the same thing said with ids

merged.means: several predecessors collapse into one successor
merged.forbids: inheriting one predecessor's id - that is picking a winner among predecessors; and reporting the losing predecessors as 'ended', which reads as fixes that never happened

unresolved.means: the evidence does not decide - the DEFAULT when evidence is absent

sides.a: a predecessor in revision A whose successor was not established: names `frm`, leaves `to` empty
sides.b: an occurrence in revision B whose predecessor was not established: names `to`, leaves `frm` null

why_symmetric: Without the b side there is no way to say 'this occurrence in B is not
explained', and an unmatched B occurrence has nowhere to go but 'new'. The
schema would then manufacture the birth event the contract forbids - the
defect would be in the vocabulary, where no implementation could avoid it.

ended.means: no successor, and the absence is POSITIVELY evidenced
ended.note: no new edge is created; a lineage the predecessor already carries is terminated, never re-minted
ended.forbids: an identity limitation as its justification - 'I found nothing' is unresolved, not a death

new.means: no predecessor, and the absence is POSITIVELY evidenced
new.forbids: an identity limitation as its justification - 'I found nothing' is unresolved, not a birth

same_pattern_id.why: pattern_id collides by design; two unrelated occurrences of one pattern share it

same_path.why: a file can hold several occurrences of the same pattern

path_rename.why: a rename relates files, not the occurrences inside them

structural_context.why: an enclosing symbol can hold several occurrences

anchored_content.why: identical content is exactly what cases 3 and 8 exploit

line_drift.why: proximity is not identity; case 8 is proximity without anything else

evidence_rule: No single evidence kind carries a 'continued' on its own.
This is a floor, not the algorithm: which COMBINATIONS suffice is slice 2
step 1 and is deliberately not fixed here.
Evidence is stored in its own field, never folded into the id and never
collapsed into a score that discards which signals fired.
limitations_rule: These say why a lineage_id is UNAVAILABLE. They belong to 'unresolved' and to
nothing else. An identity limitation is a statement about the mapper's reach;
'ended' and 'new' are statements about the world, and cannot be earned by one.
'no-predecessor-revision' means there is no revision A to compare against at
all - a first run. It must never be used while a predecessor revision exists.

containing-file-deleted.why: the file that held the occurrence is gone, so no successor can exist in it
containing-file-deleted.defeated_why: a renamed file was not deleted; it moved, and the occurrence may have moved with it

containing-file-added.why: the file did not exist in revision A, so no predecessor could have lived in it
containing-file-added.defeated_why: a file that arrived as a copy or a rename has a SOURCE; its occurrences may descend from that source, which is the branch case, not a birth

enclosing-site-removed.why: the file survives but the site does not; the occurrence has nowhere left to be
enclosing-site-removed.defeated_why: a site folded into another was not removed but relocated; the merge record says where the occurrence went

enclosing-site-added.why: the site itself is new, so the occurrence in it cannot be a continuation
enclosing-site-added.defeated_why: a site that exists because other sites were folded into it inherits their occurrences; that is the merge case, not a birth

boundary_evidence_rule: 'ended' and 'new' are EARNED, exactly like 'continued' - the difference is only
that the evidence proves an edge of the lineage rather than a link in it.
Every kind names the machine-readable field it is read from, because a boundary
asserted in prose is not a boundary: the absence of an occurrence in revision B
is precisely what 'unresolved' already covers, so it can never be the evidence
The 'boundary:' prefix keeps these impossible to confuse with an identity
limitation in a stored record, which is how the first draft went wrong.
Each kind also names what DEFEATS it. Positive evidence that is explained away
by another record is not evidence: a deleted path that appears as a rename
source did not die, and an added path that appears as a copy target was not
born. Without the defeaters, 'the file is new' would license a birth for every
copied file, and the copy case and the birth case are the same shape.

lineage_id_rules.inherit: predecessor already carries a lineage_id -> the successor takes THAT id. A re-mint would read as a new defect appearing where an old one was proven to persist.
lineage_id_rules.mint: first proven 1:1 edge between two occurrences neither of which is linked yet -> mint once, and bind BOTH ends to it.
lineage_id_rules.branch: each successor gets its own fresh child id, and every child records parent_lineage_ids. No successor inherits the predecessor's id, because inheriting is choosing.
lineage_id_rules.merge: the successor gets a freshly minted id which records parent_lineage_ids for EVERY predecessor. Inheriting one parent's id would silently elect it and orphan the rest.

lineage_id_rules_note: This is graph semantics, not an implementation detail, so it is fixed here
rather than left to the mapper. A mapper free to choose between inherit and
mint decides by itself whether a lineage survives reformatting, and a mapper
free to choose a merge id decides by itself which of several defects 'the'
surviving one is. Both are answers to questions this contract exists to ask.
What is still open is which evidence licenses each outcome - not what the ids
mapping_provenance_rule: A mapping is a statement about two specific runs over two specific revisions.
Recording both is what keeps it falsifiable outside the context that computed
it; 'mapper' is there because two mappers disagreeing about one pair of runs
is a fact worth being able to see.
A bare mapper name is not enough for that promise. Two runs of one name with
different thresholds are a disagreement that would look like a contradiction,
so the version, a digest of the configuration that was actually in force, and
the contract version the mapping was made under are all required. Without them
'would this mapping still be made under the new rule' has no answer.
preregistration_rule: Fixed BEFORE any algorithm exists, so the algorithm cannot select the cases
that flatter it. identity/tests/test_lineage_contract.py holds the matrix to
this list: a case removed or renamed fails the suite rather than disappearing.
Every one of the six outcomes must appear somewhere in the matrix, or that
outcome is frozen in name only and the mapper may implement it as it likes.
